column4: The section explicitly joins this ayah's بَعَثْنَا ... رَسُولًا to 91:12: God raises a messenger in every community, whereas Thamud's worst man launches himself; the same ayah then directs attention to the deniers' outcome.
Thamud's أَبَشَرًا مِّنَّا وَاحِدًا نَّتَّبِعُهُ states the section's decisive refusal: they scorn following the one human messenger they ought to follow.
Their reply calls the bearer of the reminder كَذَّابٌ أَشِرٌ, enacting the section's كذب sense of assigning a lie to the messenger.
The people call their صَاحِب, and that single chosen man undertakes the deed and hamstrings the camel; this is the wrong earthly following-line described in the section.
The arrogant chiefs ask whether Salih is مُرْسَلٌ مِّن رَّبِّهِ, while the believers affirm the message with which he was sent, staging both sender and followers.
After hamstringing the camel, the people challenge Salih to bring the threat إِن كُنتَ مِنَ ٱلْمُرْسَلِينَ; rejection, deed, and taunt answer the sent messenger.
كَذَّبَتْ ثَمُودُ ٱلْمُرْسَلِينَ gives the section's compressed formulation: Thamud assigns falsehood to the sent messengers.
Salih's إِنِّى لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ is the messenger's own counterword: the man they reject identifies himself as a trustworthy bearer.
The تِسْعَةُ رَهْطٍ who corrupt the city expose the organized core around Thamud's worst man, clarifying how a collective follows a destructive head.
Salih's final word, لَقَدْ أَبْلَغْتُكُمْ رِسَالَةَ رَبِّى, distinguishes the faithfully delivered message from the people's refusal to receive it.
Aad disobey their messengers and اتَّبَعُوا أَمْرَ كُلِّ جَبَّارٍ عَنِيدٍ; the ayah exactly repeats the section's two-line structure of rejecting messengers while following a ruinous chief.
Pharaoh's people فَٱتَّبَعُوا أَمْرَ فِرْعَوْنَ although his command is not right, a direct parallel to a people taking their destructive leader as the one to follow.
Pharaoh يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ and brings them into the Fire: the leader literally goes before his people and determines the destination of those behind him.
A curse is made to follow Pharaoh's people in this life and at resurrection; the repeated following turns the source-section عاقب sense into the consequence trailing the wrong line.
وَأَضَلَّ فِرْعَوْنُ قَوْمَهُ وَمَا هَدَى names the result of corrupt leadership: Pharaoh leads his people away rather than guiding them.
Pharaoh makes light of his people فَأَطَاعُوهُ; their obedience to a defiantly corrupt head closely matches Thamud's following of its worst member.
The condemned admit أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا وَكُبَرَاءَنَا فَأَضَلُّونَا ٱلسَّبِيلَا, making explicit how chiefs and great men lead their followers off the way.
Leaders who were followed disown those who followed them and all bonds are cut; it directly stages the source dictionary's ذنب branch, in which a chief's followers are his "tails."
The followers wish to return so they can disown their leaders, revealing too late the false solidarity of the human following-line described by the section.
The wrongdoer regrets not having taken a path with the Messenger, locating the fatal choice precisely between the sent guide and another companion.
The chosen companion "led me away from the Reminder after it came to me," a compact parallel to following a man who diverts one from the messenger's word.
Disbelievers tell believers ٱتَّبِعُوا سَبِيلَنَا and falsely offer to carry their sins; this is a chief's seductive counterword inviting the wrong following-line.
The inviters will carry their own burdens and burdens added to them, exposing the consequence hidden by their promise to prospective followers.
وَمَا يُمْسِكْ فَلَا مُرْسِلَ لَهُ directly realizes the section's dictionary statement that إرسال is the opposite of إمساك: what God withholds no one can release.
فَإِذَا قَرَأْنَاهُ فَٱتَّبِعْ قُرْءَانَهُ joins recitation and following in one command, precisely supporting the section's tilawa as both reading and conforming to revelation.
When revelation is recited, opponents demand a different word; the Messenger answers that he only follows what is revealed to him, uniting تلاوة, counter-speech, and faithful following.
يَتْلُونَهُ حَقَّ تِلَاوَتِهِ makes "true tilawa" the mark of belief, supporting the section's dictionary sense of reading the revealed Book by tracing its form in life.
Whoever follows divine guidance فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَىٰ; correct following is expressly protected from both straying and the شقاوة embodied by Thamud's worst man.
The Fire is entered by ٱلْأَشْقَى, repeating the section's superlative for the most wretched and attaching it to the ultimate result.
ٱلَّذِى كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ defines that "most wretched" person by denial and turning away, the same moral sequence as Thamud's rejection.
The sun cannot overtake the moon and night cannot outstrip day; each travels in an orbit, supplying the ordered celestial succession against which the section measures human following.
God sends messengers تَتْرَا, every community rejects its messenger, and He makes the communities follow one another into ruin; sending, denial, succession, and result occupy one ayah.
يَـٰأَيُّهَا ٱلرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكَ places the bearer, the borne revelation, and the duty to deliver it together, clarifying the section's paired senses of messenger and message.
Abraham asks God to ٱبْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا who will recite His signs; بعث, رسول, and تلاوة converge exactly as they do in the section's account of the sent word.
أَرْسَلْنَا فِيكُمْ رَسُولًا مِّنكُمْ يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْكُمْ ءَايَـٰتِنَا gives the إرسال counterpart to 2:129's بعث while retaining the human messenger and recited signs.
God بَعَثَ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِّنْ أَنفُسِهِمْ who recites His signs; divine raising of a human bearer contrasts with Thamud's suspicion of following a human and its man's self-launch.
بَعَثَ فِى ٱلْأُمِّيِّـۧنَ رَسُولًا مِّنْهُمْ يَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ ءَايَـٰتِهِ again binds divine commissioning, a messenger from among the people, and recitation.
God does not destroy towns until He has sent a messenger to their center reciting His signs; the ayah fixes the ethical order of message, rejection, and consequence.
وَمَا كُنَّا مُعَذِّبِينَ حَتَّىٰ نَبْعَثَ رَسُولًا sets a firm boundary: punishment follows only after God has raised a messenger.
Every community schemes to seize its messenger and disputes with falsehood; God then seizes it, reproducing the section's messenger-denial-deed-result sequence.
Those who believe in the Messenger, support him, and follow the light sent down with him succeed; both the human bearer and the sent word form the rightful following-line.
أَطِيعُوا۟ ٱلرَّسُولَ and فَإِن تُطِيعُوهُ تَهْتَدُوا۟ make obedience to the messenger the route to guidance, while his own duty is clear delivery.
ثَمُودُ بِٱلنُّذُرِ opens the parallel account with Thamud's denial of warnings, identifying what the following human objection rejects in 54:24.
God is مُرْسِلُوا۟ ٱلنَّاقَةِ as a trial and commands watchfulness and patience; the camel is itself sent into the contested obedience scene.
The water is divided and each turn is attended, supplying the exact watering-right carried in Salih's message in 91:13.
فَكَيْفَ كَانَ عَذَابِى وَنُذُرِ answers the people's taunt by joining the rejected warnings to their realized outcome.
The single blast leaves the people like dry pen-fodder, completing the consequence of following the companion who hamstrung the camel.
Salih brings clear proof, names نَاقَةُ ٱللَّهِ a sign, and forbids harming her; it is the fuller messenger-speech compressed in 91:13.
The arrogant chiefs answer the believers by declaring disbelief in the very message the believers affirm, setting the two responses to the sent word side by side.
فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ is Salih's direct claim to rightful obedience, the alternative to following the people's chosen offender.
Salih repeats فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ immediately before naming the rival command not to obey.
وَلَا تُطِيعُوا۟ أَمْرَ ٱلْمُسْرِفِينَ explicitly draws the boundary between obedience to Salih and obedience to the transgressing leaders.
The leaders whom Salih says not to obey spread corruption and do not set things right, explaining what their followers participate in.
Thamud reply that Salih is only a human like them and demand a sign, directly repeating their objection to following one human messenger.
Salih identifies the camel and assigns her and the people separate drinking days, expanding the watering claim of 91:13.
Salih forbids touching the camel with harm and warns of a tremendous day's punishment, so the consequence is stated before the choice.
They hamstring the camel and then become regretful, showing the community's participation in the chosen agent's deed.
The threatened punishment seizes them, completing this account's message-rejection-result line.
God sends Salih to Thamud, after which they become two factions disputing; the sent word immediately exposes opposed lines within the people.
They attribute their evil omen to Salih and his companions; he answers that their omen is with God, another word-against-word form of rejecting the messenger.
The nine conspirators swear together to attack Salih and his family and then lie about witnessing it, displaying the destructive leadership group's coordinated action and speech.
Their plot meets God's counter-plan while they are unaware, marking the boundary between self-directed human scheming and divine disposal.
The reader is told to look at the عَـٰقِبَةُ مَكْرِهِمْ: the consequence of the leaders' plot is their destruction with their people.
Their houses lie empty because of their wrongdoing, making the wrong following-line's collective end visible in the landscape.
God saves those who believed and were mindful, preserving the opposite community from the one organized around the nine corrupters.
God sends Thamud their brother Salih, who calls them to their Lord; it restages the human messenger's divine commission and speech.
The people answer Salih that he had inspired hope before he challenged their fathers' worship, exposing inherited allegiance as the rival to his message.
Salih grounds his speech in clear proof and mercy from his Lord and asks who could help him if he disobeyed, defining his own fidelity to the Sender.
Salih calls the camel God's sign, tells them to let her feed, and forbids harm, giving the full content of the messenger's command in 91:13.
After they hamstring her, Salih gives them three days and calls the threat a promise that will not be belied, shifting their charge of lying toward the coming verification.
When God's command comes, Salih and those who believe with him are saved; correct allegiance separates them from the collective result.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers and leaves them fallen in their homes, the consequence of the deed carried out under their leader.
The conclusion names Thamud's denial of their Lord and their removal, making rejection rather than the single man's hand the community's defining act.
God gives Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wrong her; the ayah explains that sent signs warn, linking the messenger's object to its purpose.
God guides Thamud, but they prefer blindness over guidance, and the thunderbolt takes them; their wrong preference gives the inner form of the false following-line.
Thamud are told to enjoy themselves only until a stated time, placing a measured warning before their final refusal.
They insolently defy their Lord's command and the thunderbolt takes them while they look on, joining rejected command and result.
After the punishment they cannot even rise or help themselves; their inability to stand forms a pointed aftermath to the self-rising ٱنۢبَعَثَ of 91:12.
God makes Pharaoh's party leaders who call to the Fire; the ayah states in general form what the section shows through a chief who takes those behind him to ruin.
A curse is made to follow those leaders in this world and disgrace follows on resurrection, extending the leader-follower chain into its outcome.
The weak tell the arrogant that without them they would have believed, a judgment-day disclosure of how social leaders blocked the sent word.
The arrogant ask whether they forcibly barred guidance after it came, preserving the leaders' attempt to evade responsibility for their influence.
The weak answer that the leaders' night-and-day scheming commanded disbelief, and both sides conceal regret when punishment appears; followers and chiefs share the result.
In the Fire the weak ask the arrogant leaders to relieve part of the punishment because they had been followers, realizing the section's "tails of chiefs" image.
The arrogant answer that all are in the Fire and judgment is settled, showing that leadership cannot save the people it drew behind it.
A man comes running from the farthest part of the city and says ٱتَّبِعُوا۟ ٱلْمُرْسَلِينَ; this self-mobilized man's righteous intervention reverses Thamud's worst man's initiative.
ٱتَّبِعُوا۟ مَن لَّا يَسْـَٔلُكُمْ أَجْرًا وَهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ supplies the explicit reason to follow the messengers: they seek no payment and are themselves guided.
The town rejects its messengers as mere humans and says they are lying, reproducing Thamud's objection while marking it as the unbelievers' response.
The chiefs claim that obeying a human like themselves would make the people losers, nearly restating Thamud's scorn at following one human from among them.
When messengers bring clear proofs, people ask whether humans will guide them, then disbelieve and turn away; the objection and its consequence mirror Thamud's choice.
People reject guidance by asking whether God has sent a human as messenger; the ayah identifies the same false premise behind Thamud's question.
The reply says that if angels dwelt securely on earth, an angel messenger would be sent; human messengers fit human addressees, reversing the people's objection.
The messengers acknowledge that they are humans like their hearers but say God favors whom He wills; divine sending, rather than species, establishes whom to follow.
God has بَعَثَ لَكُمْ طَالُوتَ مَلِكًا: a leader is raised for the people by God, providing a contrast to the uncommissioned worst man who launches himself.
Saul's followers are tested at the river and only a few remain disciplined; the divinely appointed leader's line is distinguished by obedience under trial.
The sun and moon are brought together at the end, a specific boundary and reversal of the ordered succession represented by the moon following the sun.
The Quran is not sent down لِتَشْقَىٰ; the revelation that should be followed is expressly dissociated from the شقاوة embodied by Thamud's worst man.
Turning away from God's reminder brings a constricted life and blind resurrection, completing the negative side of 20:123's promise to one who follows guidance.
On the coming day people divide into شَقِىٌّ وَسَعِيدٌ, explicitly confirming the section dictionary's statement that shaqwa stands opposite happiness.
Those made سُعِدُوا۟ are in the Garden, supplying the positive destination opposite the wretched line.
The reminder is avoided by ٱلْأَشْقَى, joining the superlative "most wretched" to refusal of the very word one should heed.
That most-wretched person enters the great Fire, giving the outcome of avoiding the reminder.
Disbelievers follow falsehood while believers follow the truth from their Lord; one ayah explicitly lays out the two opposed following-lines that structure the section.
When told to follow what God has sent down, people choose instead what they found their fathers following; sent revelation and inherited human allegiance compete directly.
The call to what God sent down and to the Messenger is answered by preferring ancestral practice, another exact reversal of whom and what should be followed.
People refuse the command to follow what God sent down and choose their fathers even when Satan is inviting them to the Blaze, exposing the destination of the rival line.
Whenever a warner is sent, affluent leaders say they found their fathers on a way and follow their traces; the chiefs articulate inherited following against divine sending.
Even when the warner offers better guidance than the ancestral path, the leaders declare disbelief in what he was sent with, joining wrong following to explicit rejection.
They found their fathers astray, identifying that the inherited leaders were already off course.
They are made to hurry عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَـٰرِهِم, a vivid wrong succession that enacts the section's عاقب gloss of coming in another's tracks.
One who opposes the Messenger after guidance is clear and follows a way other than the believers' is left to that choice and enters Hell; messenger and chosen route are inseparable.
God withholds the souls whose death He decrees and يُرْسِلُ ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ until a term; the bodily scene gives another concrete Quranic realization of إرسال against إمساك.
God يُرْسِلُ ٱلرِّيَـٰحَ, they raise clouds, and He spreads them through the sky; physical sending becomes motion and extension, the source section's named ر س ل root sense.
وَٱلْمُرْسَلَـٰتِ عُرْفًا evokes beings or winds sent forth in ordered succession, bringing the section's sending and following motifs into one compact image.
Within the sequence begun by the sent ones of 77:1, these agents cast a reminder; this ayah supplies the borne word that completes that neighbouring dispatch scene.
The Quran is called قَوْلُ رَسُولٍ كَرِيمٍ, placing "word" and "messenger" together and illuminating the section's distinction between the carried saying and its carrier.
Again revelation is قَوْلُ رَسُولٍ كَرِيمٍ, here in a passage describing a powerful, obeyed, trustworthy bearer; the message reaches its hearer through a commissioned carrier.
Moses and Aaron say إِنَّا رَسُولُ رَبِّ ٱلْعَـٰلَمِينَ with a singular رسول for their joint commission; this can reflect the source dictionary's message/commission sense alongside its bearer sense.
God discloses the unseen only to an approved messenger and stations guards before and behind him, protecting the transmission that 72:28 says is delivered.
The purpose is to establish that the messengers أَبْلَغُوا۟ رِسَـٰلَـٰتِ رَبِّهِمْ; borne messages and their bearers are distinguished yet joined.
Every community has a messenger, and when its messenger comes judgment is made justly; it restates the universal sending-and-outcome relation of 16:36.
No community is without a warner, supporting the section's universal horizon for the sent bearer beyond Salih and Thamud.
The inhabitants of the Fire admit that a warner came but they denied him and said God had sent nothing; their own words connect rejected sending to the outcome.
Messengers from among the hearers are said to have recited God's signs and warned of the encounter; the addressees acknowledge their own rejection.
God raises prophets as bearers of good news and warning and sends the Book with them, a broad statement of commissioned bearers carrying a revealed word.
A witness يَتْلُوهُ follows clear proof, while the Book of Moses precedes as guide and mercy; the root ت ل و operates inside a chain of revelation and testimony.
Those who listen to the word and follow its best are the ones God guides, giving the positive reception of a carried saying that Thamud refuses.
The blessed Book is followed by the command فَٱتَّبِعُوهُ; it states plainly that a sent scripture calls for enacted following.
The hearer is commanded to follow the best of what has been sent down before punishment comes suddenly, preserving the section's order of word, response, and result.
God causes messengers to follow عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَـٰرِهِمْ after Noah and Abraham, a righteous succession that exactly enacts the source-section عاقب gloss of coming in another's trace.
Jesus is sent عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَـٰرِهِمْ confirming the Torah before him; messenger and revelation occupy an ordered line of faithful succession.
After giving Moses the Book, God follows him with successive messengers, again pairing scripture with a properly ordered messenger-chain.
The sun runs toward its appointed limit by divine determination, providing the ordered first member of the sun-moon sequence completed in 36:39-40.
The moon is assigned measured phases, supplying the second celestial body whose course 36:40 protects from collision or overtaking.
Night, day, sun, and moon each swim in an orbit; the same celestial objects display rule-governed movement rather than destructive competition.
ٱلشَّمْسُ وَٱلْقَمَرُ بِحُسْبَانٍ states that sun and moon move by calculation, reinforcing the measured order behind the moon's following.
The sun is radiance and the moon light with measured stations so years and reckoning can be known; their ordered relation makes sequence intelligible to human beings.
God makes night and day a succession, خِلْفَةً, for one who wishes to remember or give thanks; orderly alternation becomes an ethical invitation.
Thamud and Aad deny the striking calamity, reducing the same historical scene to denial of the announced event.
Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming blast, supplying the result that follows the denial named in 69:4.
God saves those who believe and remain mindful, completing the direct contrast to Thamud's preference for blindness in 41:17.
The weak followers ask the arrogant leaders whether they can avert any punishment; the exchange exposes the impotence of the "heads" whose "tails" followed them.
Obeying most people on earth would lead the addressee away from God's way; numerical following supplies no warrant for the direction taken.
The Messenger is told not to obey one whose heart neglects remembrance and who follows desire, a boundary against allowing a disordered person to set the line.
God's straight path is to be followed, while other paths are not, because they disperse followers from His way; it abstracts the section's two trajectories into a rule.
The command to travel and see عَـٰقِبَةُ ٱلْمُكَذِّبِينَ repeats the exact outcome-of-deniers formula highlighted by the section.
Again the hearer must travel and look at عَـٰقِبَةُ ٱلْمُكَذِّبِينَ, turning consequence into the trace by which earlier rejection is read.
The condemned say غَلَبَتْ عَلَيْنَا شِقْوَتُنَا and admit they were astray, joining wretchedness to the path they collectively took.
